summary:
Same-sex conduct is decriminalised in Belize. On 10 August 2016 the Supreme Court, presided over by Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin, declared the colonial-era Section 53 of the Criminal Code unconstitutional in the challenge filed in 2010 by LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco and heard in Belize City in May 2013. The Human Dignity Trust carries the case in its documentation of constitutional challenges to anti-sodomy statutes, and Belize was the first former British Caribbean territory to overturn such a law.

The ruling was upheld on 30 December 2019 by the Court of Appeal, which confirmed that the Constitution's protections against discrimination extend to sexual orientation and that freedom of expression encompasses sexual expression. A visitor therefore faces no criminal exposure for consensual same-sex conduct.

Entry remains governed by Section 5(1)(e) of the Immigration Act, which lists "any prostitute or homosexual" among prohibited immigrants. Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson filed a challenge in 2013, obtained leave from the Caribbean Court of Justice in May 2014, and was joined by CARICOM as an interested party in October 2014; on 10 June 2016 the Caribbean Court of Justice dismissed the case, finding no violation of his freedom of movement. Belize argued in that litigation that Section 5(1) reaches only persons offering sexual services for financial gain and is not applied as a blanket prohibition on homosexual immigrants. The court's 10 June 2016 judgment further clarified that neither Belize nor Trinidad and Tobago may bar homosexual nationals of CARICOM states from entering, given obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas.

Statutory protection against identity-based harm exists. The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 expressly covers sexual harassment regardless of sexual preference and gender identity, and Section 8(1)(c)(i) of the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024 makes bias, prejudice or hate based on sexual orientation an aggravating circumstance in sentencing, effective 27 April 2024.

Official protection machinery is stated in commitments accepted during Belize's 2018 Universal Periodic Review: police training to respond properly to violence, measures to counter discrimination, violence and hate crimes, educational campaigns against societal stigma, and steps toward universal access to HIV treatment for LGBT people. Enforcement of these commitments by Belizean police and agencies is not documented in the sources at hand.

Public hostility has been organised and at times violent. The Supreme Court case was heard amid violence and death threats directed at LGBT activists, and religious bodies campaigned openly against decriminalisation. Visitors should expect visible social conservatism even though the law no longer criminalises same-sex conduct.
tangentialFactors:
A 2013 UNAIDS survey of 773 Belizeans aged 18 to 64 found 34% accepting and 34% tolerant of homosexuals, among the highest acceptance rates recorded in Caribbean polling, which situates Belize toward the more tolerant end of the regional distribution.

Reporting on daily life holds that gay travellers have long found Belize friendly, while arguing that the rarely enforced Section 53 had nonetheless fostered intolerance; a 1998 protest against a gay cruise docking is cited as evidence of residual public hostility.

Belize held its first Pride Week in August 2017 with awareness and acceptance activities hosted around the country, and LGBT organisations have become more visible and active since the August 2016 ruling. UNIBAM is the established national advocacy organisation.

Belize was the first CARICOM country to accept that many sexual-orientation and gender-identity recommendations in a Universal Periodic Review, accepting 15 of 17 in 2018 while noting rather than accepting two recommendations on equality of rights.
localsOnly:
On 17 August 2016 the Government said it would not appeal the Section 53 ruling, then reversed course after meeting religious leaders on 9 September and filed a partial appeal against the declaration that the Constitution bars discrimination based on sexual orientation. The Catholic Church withdrew from the appeal in March 2018, leaving the Government as sole appellant. Solicitor General Nigel Hawke argued that the ruling was judicial overreach in reading "sex" to include sexual orientation.

Religious bodies organised sustained public opposition. The Council of Churches held a "Take a Stand" rally on 3 December 2011 and a "Belize Action/Family Forum" rally on 23 November 2011 that described decriminalisation as "an orchestrated plan of demonic darkness". In December 2011 Prime Minister Dean Barrow publicly rejected pressure from US President Barack Obama, stating that Belize would not change its laws.

In its 2018 Universal Periodic Review Belize accepted 15 of 17 recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity, pledging legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and SOGI data collection. Two rights-equality recommendations were noted rather than accepted. The accepted recommendations came mostly from Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Chile, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Mexico, Spain, Ukraine, the United States and Uruguay.

Residents who are LGBT report greater organisational visibility since 2016, with UNIBAM and other groups running public programming around the August 2017 Pride Week.
outOfScopeNotes:
Prison conditions for LGBT and trans detainees remain unresolved. The encyclopedia source surveyed was fetched successfully but its only Belize content is a navigation link; it contains no Belize-specific practice on housing by birth sex versus gender identity, no trans special units, and no solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners. No placement finding can be stated.

No youth- or minor-specific findings on care, medication or travel appear anywhere in the source inventory for Belize.

Whether the pledges accepted in the 2018 Universal Periodic Review, including anti-discrimination legislation and police training, have been enacted or funded is not sourced. The two recommendations noted rather than accepted are not identified in the inventory.

The sources do not document enforcement practice under Section 5(1)(e) of the Immigration Act against individual visitors since the 2016 Caribbean Court of Justice judgment, so the practical screening risk at the border is unverified.
